397	## 10. Delivery plan and acceptance criteria
398	
399	### Spike 22 — `spikes/22-remote-port`
400	
401	Before any host code, with measured results in its README:
402	
403	- A blocking HTTPS server over `std::net::TcpListener` with `rustls` and an `rcgen` certificate, a WebSocket upgrade with `tungstenite`, and requests handed to a stand-in "frame" thread over a bounded `mpsc`, as the control socket does. Measure request latency through the handoff at the app's frame rate while hidden.
404	- **Frame cost, measured, with targets.** The frame's share of a metadata request, a content handle lookup, a worker's version action and the read-model diff over a few hundred records, each timed per pass; the target is under 1 ms per pass for the port's whole share, and under 4 ms at the 99th percentile with 8 requests in a pass. The content work on the connection thread timed separately: the largest transcript in the user's data directory parsed and masked (its time and peak memory are the supported size for §4.3), a 768 KiB file read and masked, a Keychain read made slow (a locked keychain) and shown to stall only its connection. A stalled subscriber and 20 connections that stall after the TLS handshake, with a healthy paired client and the frame loop measured through both. The README records the numbers and the thresholds, and a pass that misses the target is a design finding, not a tuning note.
405	- **Content versions.** The signals of §4.4 against the cases that defeat weaker ones: a same-size in-place rewrite of a pinned file with mtime restored by `touch -r`, a replace-by-rename, a run log truncated and regrown to the same length, a transcript appended within one poll interval; each must move the version. The two-second `stat` poll over 128 keys timed.
406	- Bonjour advertisement from the Rust process on macOS, visible to a visionOS simulator; the crate or system path that works.
407	- `URLSession` and `URLSessionWebSocketTask` on visionOS accepting the self-signed certificate through a pinning delegate that checks the SPKI hash and nothing weaker; the same delegate refusing a substituted certificate.
408	- The `openat` walk of §4.3 through `rustix` or `cap-std`: a pinned FIFO with no writer refused at once on its connection thread while the frame loop and a second connection keep going; a parent directory swapped for a symlink mid-walk refused.
409	- Two instances on one machine (`SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR`, `SWITCHBOARD_TMUX_SOCKET=switchboard-test-*`, different ports) each advertising with its own key.
410	
411	Loopback-only and no auth are fine here and nowhere else.
412	
413	**Results (2026-10-12, `spikes/22-remote-port/README.md`).** The host
414	half ran: the frame's share is under 0.25 ms per pass against the 1 ms
415	target; a request's latency is one frame interval, since a client that
416	sends on the reply synchronizes with the frame; the pools, the 5 s
417	handshake timeout and the subscriber overflow behave as §4.1 says under
418	20 stalled connections and an unread socket, with a paired client
419	unaffected; a wrong pin fails at the handshake; `mdns-sd` advertises
420	and `dns-sd` sees it; the 146 MB largest transcript parses in 290 ms at
421	575 MB peak, which is why content work is off the frame; ctime and
422	inode catch the same-size rewrite, the rename and the regrown log. Two
423	amendments follow: content reads go to **one worker thread** with a
424	queue rather than each connection thread, so one large parse is in
425	memory at a time (§4.1 is read with that change), and the Bonjour
426	instance name carries a short id suffix beside the display name. Not
427	run: the visionOS pinning delegate and the read-model diff timing.
428	
429	### Milestone A — Host port and multi-host client foundation
430	
431	Five commits, each leaving the app running and each with its README and design.md status update. The first user-visible result is a two-host read-only client at A2; nothing waits for the synchronization machinery.
432	
433	**A0 — The conversation cache in the app.** `UiState.conversations` moves to `SwitchboardApp` as the first content cache, keyed by record id, resume handle and content version; the session, card and workflow views read it through a reference. No port code. Acceptance: the UI tests pass unchanged and the app behaves identically.
434	
435	**A1 — Identity and an authenticated read-only host.** `identity.json` (id, certificate, `server_name` and the listen preference: off the LAN by default, loopback until enabled), the key in the Keychain under its installation's account, `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT`. `ports::remote`, `adapters/remote.rs` with the bounds of §4.1 and the two-step content handoff, a fake, the `Effect` and `AppAction` arms, the allowlist, the redaction function. The pairing window and QR code in the settings menu, the paired-devices dialog with scope and Revoke, `devices.json`. Endpoints: `/info`, `/pair`, projects, spaces, sets, one set, sessions, session, waiting, screen. No events yet; a reply carries `epoch` and `revision` from the counter, which only the diff of A3 will move. The screen is answered on the frame as the control port answers it (a pane snapshot, redacted); the worker handoff arrives with the screen cache of A4, since there is nothing to version before it. *Built 2026-10-12; see design.md's remote client status.* Tests: `tests/remote.rs` against a real socket with fakes, modelled on `tests/control.rs`, covering pairing, the pin check, scope, revocation, the allowlist and screen redaction; a UI test for the dialog. Acceptance: a paired `curl` with the pinned certificate reads every view over the LAN; an unpaired one gets `/info` and nothing else.
436	
437	**A2 — Two hosts and the first client.** Bonjour advertisement and the Linux stub. The Swift protocol, transport with the pinning delegate, `ServerRegistry`, `ConnectionManager`, and a read-only browser of sessions and sets with source labels, refreshing on a timer. *Built 2026-10-12 as the package under `client/` with a command-line browser for the Mac; the app targets come with Milestone B; see design.md's remote client status.* Acceptance: two installations have distinct `server_id`s and keys; Bonjour discovers both; the client pairs with both and connects simultaneously; nothing mixes identifiers; taking one offline leaves the other working and its items visibly stale; a changed IP reconnects under the same pin.
438	
439	**A3 — Synchronization.** The read-model diff after every pass, the revision counter moving, `changed` and `removed` events for metadata and collections, the WebSocket with `hello`, subscribe-then-snapshot and reconciliation by revision on the client, epoch handling, `resync_required`. `ops` and the log-before-run path in `serve` (no commands yet, but the path is tested here). *Built 2026-10-12; see design.md's remote client status. A global collection's `id` is the empty string; the diff runs only on passes that dispatched something; the `runs` collection waits for its endpoint.* Acceptance: the timer refresh of A2 is gone and every host-side change reaches the client within a pass; the mutation-between-hello-and-snapshot test passes on both sides.
440	
441	**A4 — Watched content.** The watch set and its worker poll, `watch` and `unwatch` with `watching`, content versions for screen (the other content kinds arrive with Milestone C and use the same cache), eviction, the policy fingerprint in the cache key, the overflow close. *Built 2026-10-12; see design.md's remote client status. The worker reads a pane's whole window so a short read and the poll see one version; the policy is resolved and cached on the frame (cleared by any save or secret change) until Milestone C moves the secret reads off it; a key held only by a subscriber has no read time and goes with its last `unwatch`.* Acceptance: a watched pane's screen updates live while the host shows an unrelated view or is hidden; the abuse tests of §4.1 pass against the real adapter.
442	
443	Across A1 to A4: README (Layout, dev aids, data directory) and the design.md status section, with the trust boundary's sentence on redacted text added at A1.
444	
445	### Milestone B — Native visionOS browser
446	
447	- Grid, list and focus browsing of real sessions and sets from two hosts.
448	- Two items from different servers open as independent spatial windows.
449	- Each window offers `compact` and `screen`; the other modes arrive with Milestone C and the window says so until then.
450	- Closing a window never ends a session.
451	- Reconnect preserves open windows and refreshes them through subscribe-then-snapshot.
452	
453	*Built 2026-10-12 on the visionOS simulator, three commits (B1 the app shell on an xcodegen project, B2 card windows, B3 browsing and persistence); see design.md's remote client status. The headset itself waits on the one-time Xcode device setup.*
454	
455	### Milestone C — Interactive sessions
456	
457	- `session.conversation`, `session.last_response`, `session.runs`, `session.run_output` and `file.read` on the wire and the port, with `read_pinned` in the files adapter, `read_masked` on the transcript reader and the overlap read in `scrollback`.
458	- Conversation paging by turn, with the body cap, the oversized turn, the in-progress last turn and the rebind handled.
459	- `send`, `resume` and `trust` under `control` scope, with the operation id as the idempotency key and `/ops/{op}` on timeout.
460	- Live updates over the WebSocket through the watch set; scroll and disclosure restoration across incremental refetches and reconnects.
461	- System dictation into the text field as the initial voice input.
462	
463	*C1 and C2 built 2026-10-13 (the content endpoints but `file.read`, the conversation paged and merged, the three modes drawn), C3 the same day (`send`, `resume` and `trust` under the control scope through the control socket's `serve` and log, the op the key, `/ops/{op}` on a timeout; a control bar on a Claude session's window with a microphone button that dictates through the Speech framework; the conversation view's place, scroll and folds, kept across merges, reconnects and relaunches); see design.md's remote client status. `file.read` and the policy reads off the frame remain. C4 the same day: `file.read` (`GET projects/{id}/files/{path}`, a file some working set pins, read through the descriptor walk of §4.3 in `adapters::files::open_pinned` on the content worker, versioned by inode, change time and size, masked, refused `not_pinned`, `too_large` with its size, or `failed` for a dotenv file, a symlink or a non-text file) and the policy resolved on the worker: the frame hands the worker what names a policy (`PolicySpec`: the project environment, the sets, an epoch moved by every save and secret change) and the worker reads the dotenv files and the secret store, caching per spec, so a slow Keychain call never costs a frame. Milestone C is complete.*
464	
465	### Milestone D — Shared iPadOS shell
466	
467	- The same modules and components on iPad with platform-appropriate navigation and windows.
468	
469	*Not started; Milestones A to C merged without it (2026-10-14).*
470	
471	## 11. Tests and failure cases
472	
473	Host, in `tests/remote.rs` and the adapter's own tests unless said otherwise:
474	
475	- Two hosts produce the same `RecordId` (seeded in fakes): no collision in UI or routing (client).
476	- A host's IP changes; Bonjour rediscovers it under the same pinned key (client, spike).
477	- Two advertisements claim one `server_id` with different keys: no automatic trust or merge (client).
478	- A substituted certificate during first pairing: the client refuses to send the code; and a `/pair` carrying another host's `spki_sha256` is refused by the host.
479	- Three wrong codes from three concurrent connections close the one pairing window; a fourth, correct, is refused. A consumed code is refused on the next `/pair`. Twenty unauthenticated connections and a `/pair` flood past the per-minute cap: a paired client's requests are answered throughout, the flood gets 429 and closed sockets.
480	- After Revoke, the device's next request fails and its WebSocket is closed. After a key rotation, `devices.json` is empty, every old token fails, and the dialog says the pairings are gone; the client, seeing the new key under a known `server_id`, sends nothing and asks to pair again.
481	- A scope lowered in the dialog refuses the device's next `send`; raised, allows it; no request over the port changes a scope.
482	- A mutation dispatched between a subscriber's `hello` and its first snapshot, and another during a multi-resource sync: the client ends with the host's state (host test on the ordering, client test on the reconciliation).
483	- An older snapshot reply arriving after a newer one is dropped by revision (client).
484	- The host restarts: the new `epoch` makes the client refetch everything.
485	- A `send` whose process is killed after the keys went into the pane and before the reply line (the fake host records the write, the fake log fails the reply append): the retry with the same op is answered `interrupted` and nothing is sent twice. A failed request-line append refuses the send and sends nothing. A dropped HTTP response after a logged reply is answered from the log.
486	- `unknown` for an op that never reached the frame; a resubmit runs once.
487	- The configured secret appears in a prompt, a tool result, a final response, a run's output, and a pinned non-dotenv text file: every content endpoint returns it masked. A secret store that fails makes every content endpoint refuse rather than answer.
488	- The configured secret straddles each cut: the parser's `DETAIL_CAP` inside a tool result, the 256 KiB turn cut, the first byte of a run-output tail window, and the front cut of a last response: each reply masks it whole or drops it whole, never a fragment.
489	- A project with three hundred sessions, each with 64 KiB notes and a 100 KiB `name`, listed whole: one reply under the cap, notes cut at 4 KiB and names at 4 KiB with each field in `truncated`, no member lost; the same session read alone carries its notes whole. A session entering and leaving `waiting` emits `changed {waiting}` and the refetched collection lacks or holds it accordingly; a member missing from a whole reply at a later revision is dropped by the client, a member missing from an older reply arriving late is not.
490	- A 700 KiB file of quotation marks is under the source limit and answers `too_large` from the serialized check; a pane with 200 lines of 4 KiB each is cut by bytes after masking and marked. A pinned file over the source limit answers `too_large`; a last response over the body cap is cut from the front and marked.
491	- Content versions (F2): a pinned file rewritten in place at the same size with its mtime restored, a file replaced by rename, a run log truncated and regrown to its old length, and a transcript appended twice within one poll interval: each read after the change carries new content and a new revision, and no two different bodies for one key share a revision within an epoch. Two reads of an unchanged file carry the same revision.
492	- Frame cost (F4): a 20 MiB transcript, a 768 KiB file and a Keychain read made to block for two seconds, each requested while a second connection reads session metadata: the metadata reply arrives within a pass and the frame's time per pass stays under its budget; only the requesting connection waits. A content handle read on the frame for a record removed before the worker finishes: the worker's version action is a no-op and the reply names the handle it read.
493	- A window on the last response alone, and one on the conversation, each refresh when the transcript grows with no session metadata change; a handle rebind refreshes both.
494	- With every content cache populated, a new environment-set grant, a changed secret value, and a secret store that starts failing: unchanged screen, file and run-output sources are not served from their old masked bytes; the first two emit `changed` for the watched keys and serve newly masked text, the third refuses.
495	- A watched session's transcript grows and a watched pinned file is edited while the host shows an unrelated project, a document, the Dispatch page, and while the window is hidden: `changed` arrives within the poll interval.
496	- A space rename, a session moved between projects, a project and a session removed, a time-based rule set losing a member: the right `changed` and `removed` events, no reconnect.
497	- A set renamed and a pin moved (saved through `SaveViews`), a Claude Code pane reaching its trust question (`PromptSeen`, no save), and a Codex pane passing its quiet interval (`HostListed`, no save, no screen change): each emits `changed` for the right resource within the pass. Ten passes over a running pane with nothing else moving emit nothing, though `quiet_secs` moved on each.
498	- Two reads of a watched file, a transcript and a pane separated by an external edit with no poll between them, delivered to the client in reverse order: the client ends on the newer content. A read of a session's metadata between them does not invalidate the conversation page.
499	- Closing one of two windows on a session sends no `unwatch`; closing the second does. A hundred and twenty-nine watched keys against the cap of 128: the least recently read is evicted, a read of it still answers with the right version and re-enters it, and no watch is refused. Reconnect resends the watches before any snapshot.
500	- Forget server on the client removes its token, pin, memory and views; a revocation seen on a connection drops the token and memory and keeps the views marked; nothing from a host is found on the client's disk after a relaunch (client).
501	- The subscriber queue overflows: `resync_required`, the socket closes, the host's frame loop and a second subscriber are unaffected (spike and adapter test).
502	- 20 stalled unauthenticated connections: the port stays answerable to a paired client (spike).
503	- `read_pinned`: a pin with `..`, an absolute path, an empty component; a symlink as a parent component (inside or outside the root, both refused) and as the leaf; a parent directory swapped for a symlink between two hops of the walk, driven from a second thread; a file that grows past the limit during the read; a FIFO with no writer, asserting the refusal returns at once and an unrelated request completes meanwhile; a directory and a device as the leaf. Each refused or capped as §4.3 says.
504	- A long transcript pages by turn; one enormous turn is cut and marked; a conversation whose handle changed answers with the new `resume_id` and the client refetches from 1 (client).
505	- An exited command whose pane is gone: `screen` refuses, `runs` and `run_output` answer from the log; a pruned log answers with the reason.
506	- Several windows show one session with independent view state and consistent data (client).
507	- A request outside the allowlist (`env.resolve`, `project.add`, a path that no set pins, a pinned `.env`) is refused with no side effect, and the refusal is logged by name only.
508	- Revocation while connected: the WebSocket closes, the next request fails with the reason, cached content stays readable on the client but is marked.
509	- A restart and a rebuild under the stable signing identity keep the key readable; two data directories under one macOS account keep separate keys; a missing key makes a fresh identity and the dialog says the pairings are gone.
510	- A `cfg(not(target_os = "macos"))` build compiles with the Bonjour adapter stubbed.
511	
512	## 12. Answers to the first draft's questions
513	
514	1. **Models and ids.** `src/core/model.rs`: `SessionRecord` (`RecordId`), `Project` (`ProjectId`), `WorkingSet` (`SetId`) with `PinnedItem { target: PinTarget, rect: GridRect }`, `CardState`, `Run` (a command's or service's run with its scrollback log name). Conversations are `ports::transcript::Conversation` with `Turn { n, user, activity, final_text, .. }`, read by `adapters/transcript.rs` from Claude Code's JSONL.
515	2. **Control port reuse.** Yes, directly: `app.rs::serve` takes a `wire::Request` and returns a `wire::Reply`; `core/control.rs` maps bodies to `ControlAction`. The remote adapter is another producer of requests for the same path, with auth, the allowlist and redaction in front, and the log-before-run step added to `serve` for non-replayable commands.
516	3. **Runtime.** None to own; the frame thread is the executor and `listen`/`serve_pending` are the startup and polling hooks. Shutdown drops the listener as the control socket does.
517	4. **Events.** No bus, and no effect that reliably marks a visible change: `Save`, `SaveViews` and `SaveSettings` are three effects, and `PromptSeen` and the quiet interval in `reconcile.rs` change a card with none of them. So the port diffs the exported read models after every pass, with the clock-derived `quiet_secs` held out of the hash, and versions content where it is read (§4.4). Retained replay is not needed: a subscriber is registered on the frame thread, so subscribe-then-snapshot has no gap.
518	5. **Pinned file access.** The document preview (`ui::document::Preview::load`) is a UI loader: a metadata check and then an unbounded read, which is fine for the user's own click and not for a remote reader. The port gets `read_pinned` in the files adapter: a descriptor-anchored `openat` walk with no symlink followed and a nonblocking open, as §4.3 says, run on the connection thread.
519	6. **Per-session UI state and polling.** `UiState` (drafts, scroll, folds) is transient and never read by the core; none of it crosses to the client. The conversation cache in `UiState` and the caption poll in `refresh_captions` both follow the local view: a session not on the Mac's screen is not polled, and a document, workflow, Dispatch or ticket view polls nothing. The app also parses a transcript synchronously on the frame (`refresh_conversation`), which one frame absorbs for one session on screen and would not for every watched session. The port therefore needs its own watch set, the cache lifted to the app, and content work on the connection and worker threads, which are the app-level changes the implementation constraint allows.
520	7. **Two installations.** `SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR` and `SWITCHBOARD_TMUX_SOCKET` on a `switchboard-test-*` socket; only the lock holder listens; `tests/control.rs` and `tests/gate.rs` show the pattern.
521	
522	**Implementation constraint:** no change to the egui frontend beyond A0's cache move, and no change to how the transcript parser reads or shapes a conversation. The host work is one adapter, additive wire views, a `read_pinned` method on the files port, an additive `read_masked` on the transcript reader (the mask runs inside the existing parse, before its detail cap) and an overlap read in `scrollback`, the content caches, read-model diff, two-step content handoff and watch worker in `app.rs`, the log-before-run step in `serve`, a Settings field or two, and one dialog. Anything larger is proposed separately.
523	
524	## 13. Explicit design decisions
525	
526	| Decision | v1 choice |
527	|---|---|
528	| Topology | Independent hosts, no coordinator |
529	| Multi-host | Concurrent connections and unified browsing |
530	| Resources | Sessions, projects, working sets with pins, pinned files, runs; no card resource |
531	| Identity | `identity.json` UUID and certificate; key in the Keychain per installation; clients pin the public key |
532	| Discovery | Bonjour and manual endpoints |
533	| Host runtime | Frame-thread dispatch for core state; content work on connection and worker threads; blocking std server with bounded queues; no Tokio |
534	| Contract | The `switchboard-control` wire views, extended additively, behind an allowlist |
535	| Data fetch | HTTPS JSON, every reply stamped with epoch and revision |
536	| Live changes | One WSS per host; read-model diff after every pass, content versions assigned on read, watch worker; `changed`/`removed` events; refetch |
537	| Synchronization | Subscribe, then snapshot, then reconcile by revision; full refetch on a new epoch |
538	| Idempotency | The control port's operation id and `operations.log`, non-replayable commands logged before they run |
539	| Redaction | One policy over every text leaving the port, run on whole source text before any cut; fail closed |
540	| Caps | Collections answered whole with every string bounded; only the conversation pages; scalar content cut after masking or refused whole; the limit enforced on serialized bytes |
541	| Content versions | Transcript: size and mtime (append-only); file and run log: inode, ctime and size; screen: hash; no two bodies share a revision for one key |
542	| Masked caches | Versioned by source and by the project's redaction policy fingerprint; a resolution failure refuses, never serves a cached success |
543	| Watch set | Global cap of 128, least recently read evicted, never refused; a read always versions correctly |
544	| File reads | Descriptor-anchored `openat` walk, no symlink followed, nonblocking open, 768 KiB, on the connection thread |
545	| Authentication | Pairing window with QR, key verified before the code is sent, 40-bit single-use code with one global attempt counter, 256-bit bearer token without expiry, scope set in the host dialog; Keychain on both ends; key rotation clears every pairing |
546	| Client storage | Server list and presentation state on disk, token and pin in the Keychain, every host body in memory only |
547	| Milestone A | Five commits: cache move, authenticated read-only host, two-host client, synchronization, watched content |
548	| Session execution | Always on the owning host |
549	| Resume | User-initiated only, confirmed on the client |
550	| Presentation state | Client-owned |
551	| visionOS layout | Native movable windows |
552	| Remote internet access | Deferred; protocol-compatible |
553	| iPadOS | Shared Swift core and views |

  per key and re-reads only when the version or the policy moved; a
  watched file emits `changed {file, project/path}` on the poll.
  Refusals: `not_pinned` (404), `too_large` (413, with the size),
  `failed` (400) for a dotenv file, a symlink, a FIFO or a non-text
  file. The client holds files as content (`FileBody`, `watch(file:)`,
  re-read on `changed`); no window shows one yet, which the working set
  view brings. Milestone C is complete.
- **Scope on the listings.** A listing over the remote port leaves
  out the records Dispatch made for its own use (a ticket's project
  and its sessions, a worker session anywhere), told by the
  `<ticket>-<nonce>` op they were made under
  (`switchboard_control::is_dispatch_worker_op`); a supervisor's
  (`sup-…`) and the owner's own stay. `?scope=all` on `projects`,
  `sessions`, `waiting` and the `events` subscription lists and
  announces them, and a worker record is still read by its id, for
  the ticket view to come. Frames for a worker record go to `scope=all`
  subscribers alone. The control socket is untouched, so Dispatch sees
  everything as before.
- **On the headset (2026-10-14).** Scene restoration is ruled out: a
  launch opens the Sessions window and nothing else (the card and
  prompt window groups have `restorationBehavior(.disabled)`), after a
  restored window kept the process alive out of view so that an icon
  tap presented nothing. A launch log in the app's container
  (`launch.log`: launches, window appearances, scene phases) stands in
  for a device syslog the Mac cannot read. The conversation's end
  marker lives outside the lazy stack, so the follow button and
  opening at the end hold on the device. Following the end was then
  made a mode (2026-10-16): the view is held at the end with scrolling
  off, and anything growing under it pulls the end back on screen; a
  button at the right edge releases it to read, the ellipsis at the
  foot returns it. Before, following meant "the marker is on screen",
  and a new turn's row growing after the scroll landed pushed the
  marker off and turned following off by itself; the turn at the top
  was also a position bound to the scroll view, which re-applied it as
  the content grew and sent the view up. Markdown tables in an answer
  are laid out as grids. A Bonjour resolve that gets no answer is
  given up after 5 s, and each offline host resolves on its own task,
  after the retry loop hung on one resolve left waiting by the system.
- **Tickets on the headset (2026-10-17).** The port serves Dispatch's
  tickets from the app's own status poll (`src/core/tickets.rs`, spec
  §4.7): a listing by project with each ticket's standing worded as the
  Mac's page words it and its decisions; one ticket with its body,
  attempts and lanes; `decide` and `resume` under `control`, answered
  when Dispatch answers the call the Mac's action became
  (`TicketReply`, the content worker's deferred channel reused). The
  tickets are one fingerprinted collection, so a device hears one
  `changed tickets` frame per status that moved. The client lists them
  on a Tickets tab, oldest first within a project, urgent ones marked,
  with a detail view that answers decisions (the recommended option
  first, a note field, several options for a `multiple` one), resumes
  a parked ticket, and opens the project's supervisor session.

  Refusals: `not_pinned` (404), `too_large` (413, with the size),

  re-read on `changed`); no window shows one yet, which the working set
  view brings. Milestone C is complete.
- **Scope on the listings.** A listing over the remote port leaves
  out the records Dispatch made for its own use (a ticket's project
  and its sessions, a worker session anywhere), told by the
  `<ticket>-<nonce>` op they were made under
  (`switchboard_control::is_dispatch_worker_op`); a supervisor's
  (`sup-…`) and the owner's own stay. `?scope=all` on `projects`,
  `sessions`, `waiting` and the `events` subscription lists and
  announces them, and a worker record is still read by its id, for
  the ticket view to come. Frames for a worker record go to `scope=all`
  subscribers alone. The control socket is untouched, so Dispatch sees
  everything as before.
- **On the headset (2026-10-14).** Scene restoration is ruled out: a
  launch opens the Sessions window and nothing else (the card and
  prompt window groups have `restorationBehavior(.disabled)`), after a
  restored window kept the process alive out of view so that an icon
  tap presented nothing. A launch log in the app's container
  (`launch.log`: launches, window appearances, scene phases) stands in
  for a device syslog the Mac cannot read. The conversation's end
  marker lives outside the lazy stack, so the follow button and
  opening at the end hold on the device. Following the end was then
  made a mode (2026-10-16): the view is held at the end with scrolling
  off, and anything growing under it pulls the end back on screen; a
  button at the right edge releases it to read, the ellipsis at the
  foot returns it. Before, following meant "the marker is on screen",
  and a new turn's row growing after the scroll landed pushed the
  marker off and turned following off by itself; the turn at the top
  was also a position bound to the scroll view, which re-applied it as
  the content grew and sent the view up. Markdown tables in an answer
  are laid out as grids. A Bonjour resolve that gets no answer is
  given up after 5 s, and each offline host resolves on its own task,
  after the retry loop hung on one resolve left waiting by the system.
- **Tickets on the headset (2026-10-17).** The port serves Dispatch's
  tickets from the app's own status poll (`src/core/tickets.rs`, spec
  §4.7): a listing by project with each ticket's standing worded as the
  Mac's page words it and its decisions; one ticket with its body,
  attempts and lanes; `decide` and `resume` under `control`, answered
  when Dispatch answers the call the Mac's action became
  (`TicketReply`, the content worker's deferred channel reused). The
  tickets are one fingerprinted collection, so a device hears one
  `changed tickets` frame per status that moved. The client lists them
  on a Tickets tab, oldest first within a project, urgent ones marked,
  with a detail view that answers decisions (the recommended option
  first, a note field, several options for a `multiple` one), resumes
  a parked ticket, and opens the project's supervisor session.

content.content:
pin.txt
*.log
*.pid
accept loop dropped it); a new connection was served again 4.85 s
later, when the 5 s handshake timeout cleared the four held slots.
So an unauthenticated flood costs a new device up to 5 s and costs an
established device nothing, which is what §4.1's separate pools are
for.

**Pin.** A client pinned to another hash fails at the handshake with
"certificate is not the pinned one"; no request is sent.

**Bonjour.** `mdns-sd` registered `_switchboard._tcp` with TXT `v=1`
and the display name, and `dns-sd -B _switchboard._tcp local.` listed
"Spike 22" within the second. Note that two instances on one machine
need distinct instance names, which the display name gives.

**Transcript parse** (the app's own parser, release build, the
largest transcripts in this machine's data; peak RSS is the test
process):

| file | read | parse | turns | kept text | peak RSS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 146 MB | 55 ms | 237 ms | 402 | 1.5 MB | 575 MB |
| 80 MB | 20 ms | 84 ms | 176 | 0.46 MB | 260 MB |

So the app's comment that "several megabytes costs tens of
milliseconds" holds per megabyte, and the data directory holds
sessions a hundred times that size: **290 ms per read, or eighteen
frames, which settles §4.1: content work runs on a connection thread,
never the frame.** Memory is the whole file plus its JSON, four times
the file; the parsed conversation the cache keeps is 1.5 MB. Two of
these in flight at once is over a gigabyte of transient memory, which
argues for one content worker, not one per connection, or for a
parser that streams lines (out of scope; `§2`).

**Content versions** (`tests/versions.rs`, all pass):

- a same-size rewrite with mtime restored by `touch -r` leaves (mtime,
  size) unchanged and moves ctime;
- a replace-by-rename moves the inode;
- a log truncated and regrown to the same length moves ctime;
- an appended transcript is strictly larger after each append, so size
  alone versions it.

## Recommendation

Build the port as `docs/remote-client.md` says, with three amendments
from the numbers: the content reads go to **one worker thread** with a
queue, not to each connection thread, so that at most one large parse
is in memory at a time; the latency the client should expect is one
frame interval, so a visible view's periodic refetch need not be faster
than a few seconds; and the Bonjour instance name is the display name
plus a short id suffix when two instances share a machine.

## Left to the owner

- The `URLSession` and `URLSessionWebSocketTask` pinning delegate on
  visionOS against this server (`--bonjour` to discover it); the
  server's pin is in `pin.txt` after a run.
- The read-model diff cost over a few hundred records, which needs the
  app's views; the serialization of a few hundred small structs is
  well under the pass budget by the parse numbers above, but it is not
  measured.

# Spike 23: the page on the remote port

The questions issue #230's plan leaves to a browser, which no test in
the tree can drive: whether Chrome and Safari on the Mac store and
send a `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` cookie set by a server with
a self-signed P-256 certificate that has no subject alternative name
(the one `make_identity` makes today) on an IP-literal host once the
owner has clicked past the warning; whether two servers on two ports
of one address keep their cookies apart when each names its cookie
for its own server id; whether a WebSocket to the same origin is
admitted under `connect-src 'self'` and connects over that
certificate; and how many connections a page load opens against the
port's pool of four unauthenticated slots.

Standalone crate, not built by the app. Builds into its own
`target/`, as spike 22 does.

## What it does

`src/main.rs` is a throwaway HTTPS server: a fresh key and SAN-less
certificate per run, a page under the port's exact
Content-Security-Policy, `POST /pair` setting
`__Host-sb-<id>=token-for-<id>; Max-Age=34560000; Path=/; Secure;
HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict`, `GET /me` answering 200 when that cookie
(by its exact name) came back and 401 otherwise, and `GET /events`
answering a WebSocket upgrade with one text frame and a close. The
page shows three lines: the cookie after Pair, the cookie on a reload
(the `SameSite=Strict` case: a reload is same-site, the first open
from a camera app is not), and the socket's outcome.

## Commands

```sh
cd spikes/23-web-page
cargo run --release -- --port 43187 --id a      # one instance
```

content.content:
The second review round (the outside reviewer's F1–F6, and a trim) changed
this:

- Collections are answered whole with bounded fields; the membership
  snapshot walk is gone. Only the conversation pages.
- The watch set is capped globally with least-recently-read eviction; there
  is no `watch_refused` and no "not live" client state.
- Content work (parsing, file reads, masking, hashing) runs on the
  connection thread, never on the frame; the frame hands out the handle and
  the policy and records the version. The frame does core state only.
- Content versions for files and logs are inode, ctime and size, not mtime
  and length (F2). Pairing codes, tokens, attempt counting and key rotation
  are specified (F3). The client keeps content in memory only (F5). A client
  workspace may span hosts (F6).
- Milestone A is five commits, A0 to A4, with a two-host read-only client at
  A2 (F1).

## 1. Product goals
- **Known gaps at the first merge.** Milestone D, the iPad shell, is
  not started. The Codex transcript parser, so a Codex session's
  conversation is empty on a device. The Dispatch ticket view
  (`scope=all` is served; no view asks for it). Removing dead sessions
  from a device. The Recent sessions set counts worker sessions. The
  screen and run-output modes follow the end without the
  conversation's end marker. The draft path makes the editor on the
  frame (`prompt_box::ensure_editor` reads the voice key there), so an
  unsigned host freezes on the Keychain prompt while a device asks for
  a draft; the signed bundle never prompts. Remote access off the LAN
  is §9 of the spec, deferred.

## Versioning and updates (2026-10-15)

lines: - **Bounds.** The port is one user's few devices, and the limits say so:
- at most 16 connections in total and 4 unauthenticated ones; a further accept is closed at once. The 4 are a separate pool: an unauthenticated flood fills its own slots and never a paired client's;
- `/pair` is answered at most six times a minute per listener and `/info` sixty; past that the connection thread answers 429 without reaching the frame;

+  - the page's three files (`GET /`, `/app.js`, `/app.css`, matched exactly) are answered on the connection thread as constant bytes, never through the frame, with `Connection: close` so a load frees its unauthenticated slot at once; they have a window of their own, 120 a minute per listener (a load is three), 429 past it. A page request counts in the unauthenticated pool from accept like any stranger's;
- a TLS handshake and the first request line each within 5 s, a request body within 10 s, a write within 10 s; a connection that misses a deadline is closed;
- one request in flight per connection (HTTP/1.1, no pipelining);

- the frame drains at most 8 remote requests per pass, in arrival order, the rest waiting on the channel; the channel is bounded at 64 and a full channel answers 503 from the connection thread without reaching the frame; a frame-side request is a view or a handle lookup and takes microseconds, so the count is the bound;

lines: New read models, added to the wire crate:

- `session.conversation`: the `Conversation` from `ports::transcript` as a wire shape: title, model, branch, usage, and turns paged by **turn number** (`n`, 1-based). The host parses the whole JSONL, as the session view does, from the app-level cache (§4.4); a transcript the app can show is one the port can serve, and the supported size is whatever the app handles, which the spike measures. What paging bounds is the **response**: a page anchored at its start (`from=turn`) stops at `limit` turns or at the body cap, whichever first, and says `next` for the turn to continue from; a page anchored at its end (`from=last`, or `before=turn` for the page ending before a turn the client holds) fills backward from the anchor, so it always reaches it and `from` is wherever it filled up. The client opens on the tail and walks back with `before`, so a transcript whose turns are large never shows a stale end or a gap; a change is followed from the last turn held page after page until `next` is empty, up to ten pages. A page carries only the first 512 bytes of each tool call's input and result and of each activity's text, marked `more`, which is what keeps a turn with a hundred tool calls to tens of kilobytes rather than hundreds; `session.turn` reads one turn whole, at the conversation's revision, and the client asks for it when a turn's activity is opened. A single turn larger than 256 KiB is cut (final text kept whole where possible, activity text trimmed) and marked `truncated`. The page carries the `resume_id` it was read from: `/clear` and a discard rebind the record to a new transcript, and a client holding turn numbers from another handle drops them and refetches from 1. The last turn is always in progress until a `Stop` event: on a `changed {conversation}` the client refetches from the last turn it holds and **replaces** that turn and everything after it. A handle rebind (`resume_id` moved on the session view) changes the conversation cache's key, which emits `changed {conversation}` of its own, so the client needs no rule linking the two. Only Claude Code sessions have a conversation; Codex, shell, command and service sessions answer with a "no conversation" reason and the client falls back to `screen` (and, for commands and services, `run_output`).

-- `session.last_response`: the last turn's `final_text`, its `n` and `end`. It is a **projection of the `conversation` key**: it is read from the same cache, carries the conversation's content revision, is watched by watching `conversation`, and refreshes on `changed {conversation}`; a window showing only the last response registers that watch. The compact card's one-line excerpt is not part of it: that is `last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the session's metadata, and moves with `changed {session}`.

The compact card's one-line excerpt is not part of it, and is not on the port yet: the Mac computes it in the UI from the transcript (`src/ui/cards.rs`), the record keeps only the `Stop`'s time, and `SessionView` has no excerpt field. Putting it on the wire is an additive `SessionView` field with the function moved into the core, a follow-up (2026-10-23).

- `session.runs`: a command's or service's runs as the record holds them (`Run`: `n`, started, ended, exit, artifacts' names, not their paths). `session.run_output`: the tail of one run's scrollback log (`scrollback::tail_text`, escapes stripped, `lines` clamped to 500), redacted; a run whose log was pruned or rotated answers with that reason. This is how an exited command whose pane is gone is still readable: `session.screen` refuses a session that is not running, by design.

- `file.read`: content of a file **only if some working set pins it** (`PinTarget::File` with that project and path). The read goes through a new `ports::files` method, `read_pinned(root, relative)`, not through the UI's preview loader. Confinement is by descriptors, not by path strings, so it stays valid while names change under it:
- the relative path is rejected if it is absolute, empty, or has a `..` or `.` component, before anything touches the disk (a persisted pin can hold anything);

lines: A local network is not a trust boundary: these APIs can instruct coding agents and expose private transcripts. The repo's rules apply unchanged: secret values never reach a record, a log line, a command line, or any reply but `env.resolve` (which is not on this port) and, as redacted text, the read models of §4.3; the Keychain holds key material.
+- Require pairing **before** anything but `/info`, `/pair` and the page's three files (`/`, `/app.js`, `/app.css`), which are constant bytes.

- **Host identity**: a self-signed certificate made once with `rcgen` on first listen. The certificate is in `identity.json` (§3.1); its private key is a Keychain item through the existing adapter (`adapters/keychain.rs`, service `com.sadburger.switchboard`) under the account `remote-key:<server_id>`, so two data directories under one macOS account never overwrite each other's keys. The bundle must be signed with the stable identity (`scripts/bundle.sh`) or the Keychain ACL is lost on every rebuild.

- **What the client pins** is the SPKI SHA-256 of the host's public key, not the certificate's bytes, so a certificate reissued from the same key (a new expiry) still verifies. Rotating the key is making a new identity: every pairing is invalid and the dialog says so.

- **Pairing verifies the key before the code is sent.** The code alone would let an intermediary terminate the first connection, forward the code to the real host, and take the token. So the pairing window shows a **QR code** carrying `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`, and under it the same in text: a short form of the key hash and the code. The client scans or types both; it connects, compares the hash of the key it is actually talking to with the one it was given, and only when they match sends `/pair {code, device_name, spki_sha256}`. A client without a camera (visionOS gives an app none) pairs from the host's Bonjour record instead: it resolves the record, reads `/info` under no trust, shows the key the host presented in the dialog's short form for the owner to compare by eye, and pins that key for the pairing, so the typed code reaches only the host whose key the owner checked; a substituted certificate shows its own key on the device, where the owner sees it differ. The host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is not its own, so a relayed request through a substituted certificate fails even if the code reached it. Before pairing, `/info` is served to any client and nothing in it is trusted; after pairing, every connection verifies the pin before the token is presented.

input.new_string:
- **The token**: 32 bytes from the OS random source, base64url, 43 characters. It does not expire; the owner revokes. It is sent only as a bearer header over the pinned connection, or as the cookie below, never in a URL.
- `/pair` answers with the token and the granted scope. The host stores the device name, scope, created time, last-seen time and the token's SHA-256 in `<data dir>/devices.json` (atomic write, owner-readable); never the token. The client stores the token and the pinned key hash in its Keychain.
- **A browser's credential is a cookie** (2026-10-23). `/pair` with `"transport": "cookie"` in its body answers with `Set-Cookie: __Host-sb-<server_id>=<token>; Max-Age=34560000; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` and a body without `token`, so the page's script never holds it; a native client omits the field and is unchanged. The host accepts the cookie named `__Host-sb-<its own server_id>` as a credential beside the bearer header (the bearer wins when both are present; every other cookie is ignored). The name carries the id because cookies ignore ports: two instances on one Mac share a jar for the page's host, and a fixed name would have the second pairing overwrite the first; the id is stable across a key rotation, so a rotation does not orphan the cookie. lines: - **Pairing verifies the key before the code is sent.** The code alone would let an intermediary terminate the first connection, forward the code to the real host, and take the token. So the pairing window shows a **QR code** carrying the page's URL, `https://<address>:<port>/#code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>` (2026-10-23; before, the JSON `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`, which the Swift client's `PairingInvite.parse` still accepts), and under it the same in text: a short form of the key hash and the code. The three values travel in the URL's fragment, which a browser never sends in a request, so a server the owner has not verified never receives the code; the page compares `/info`'s key and id with the fragment's before it sends anything. The client scans or types both; it connects, compares the hash of the key it is actually talking to with the one it was given, and only when they match sends `/pair {code, device_name, spki_sha256}`. **A browser cannot pin**: it cannot see which certificate it is talking to, so the comparison catches a QR for another host or a stale one and is not a defence against a relay that terminates TLS; the trust step for a browser is proceeding past the certificate warning, and the dialog says to pair a browser only on a network you trust. The URL names the machine's local address only while the port listens on the network, and the loopback address otherwise, with the dialog saying the port is this Mac's alone. A client without a camera (visionOS gives an app none) pairs from the host's Bonjour record instead: it resolves the record, reads `/info` under no trust, shows the key the host presented in the dialog's short form for the owner to compare by eye, and pins that key for the pairing, so the typed code reaches only the host whose key the owner checked; a substituted certificate shows its own key on the device, where the owner sees it differ. The host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is not its own, so a relayed request through a substituted certificate fails even if the code reached it. Before pairing, `/info` is served to any client and nothing in it is trusted; after pairing, every connection verifies the pin before the token is presented.

- The pairing window is opened from the settings menu as "Allow pairing for 5 minutes", the same shape as the environment setup window (`ENV_SETUP_WINDOW`, never saved). The dialog that opens it chooses the scope the pairing grants, `read` by default.

- **The code**: eight characters from the 32-character Crockford alphabet (no `I`, `L`, `O`, `U`), 40 bits, drawn from the OS random source (`getrandom`), made when the window opens and shown as the QR's `code` and in text. It is single-use: the first successful `/pair` consumes it and closes the window. **Failures count globally**: one counter in the app's state, bumped on the frame for every failed `/pair` from any connection, and the window closes at three. Concurrent attempts cannot each get three, because the frame answers them in arrival order against the one counter.
-- **The token**: 32 bytes from the OS random source, base64url, 43 characters. It does not expire; the owner revokes. It is sent only as a bearer header over the pinned connection, never in a URL.

Revocation removes the record, takes effect on the next request and closes the device's WebSocket.

input.new_string:
a draft; the signed bundle never prompts. Remote access off the LAN
  is §9 of the spec, deferred.
- **A web page on the port (2026-10-23).** The port serves three
  embedded files (`web/index.html`, `app.js`, `app.css`, the table in
  `src/adapters/web.rs`) from the connection thread as constant bytes,
  never through the frame, with `Connection: close` so a load frees
  its unauthenticated slot at once, a window of 120 a minute, and a
  Content-Security-Policy that admits only the page's own files and
  origin. The pairing window's QR code is now the page's URL with the
  code, key hash and server id in its fragment (`core::remote::
  invite_url`), which a browser never sends in a request; the page
  compares `/info` with the fragment, pairs with `transport: "cookie"`
  and gets its token as an `HttpOnly` cookie named `__Host-sb-<server
  id>` (so two instances on one Mac keep their cookies apart), which
  the host accepts beside the bearer header; a cookie write or upgrade
  must carry the page's `Origin`. `GET /me` tells the page its scope.
  The page lists the sessions with the waiting ones first, shows a
  Claude Code session's last response or any other's screen, and sends
  a reply under `control`; it polls `/waiting` every three seconds as
  its base and uses the events socket when a browser connects it
  (Safari is not expected to, over a self-signed certificate). The
  Swift client's `PairingInvite.parse` takes the URL and the older
  JSON. Known gaps: the browser's trust step is clicking past the
  certificate warning, which no test drives (`spikes/23-web-page`
  lists the five browser steps, not run); a trusted-certificate path
  is a follow-up of its own; the card's one-line excerpt is not on
  the wire, so a row shows the name, kind, card word, waiting reason
  and time since activity; `history.replaceState` clears the fragment
  from the address bar, and whether Safari keeps it in an earlier
  history entry is unknown, which the code's single use covers.

# Changelog

Every user-visible change goes under Unreleased as it lands.
`scripts/bump.sh` moves that section under the next version with the
date, and `scripts/release.sh` publishes that section as the release
notes. The format follows [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com)
and the versions follow [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org).

## [Unreleased]

## [0.4.1] - 2026-10-21

- Dispatch takes an issue once per project rather than once across the data directory, so a second project on the same repository can take an issue the first already holds.

## [0.4.0] - 2026-10-21

### Added

- Dispatch reports each ticket's tokens by model and agent time, per attempt, stage and ticket, in `dispatch report` and a Usage tab on the ticket page.

### Fixed

- The session page's token count counts each message once, not once per content block, skips Claude Code's synthetic messages, and names each model when a session used more than one.

## [0.3.0] - 2026-10-19

### Added

- A session can be opened from the headset: a plus button on the Sessions tab, or "New session in this project" on a listed session, opens a Claude Code, Codex or shell session in a project on any connected host paired under the control scope, in the project's root or a directory under it, with a first message for an agent; the new session's window opens on the reply. The remote port takes `POST projects/{id}/sessions` for it and lists `create` among its capabilities.
- The remote port serves Dispatch's tickets: a listing with each ticket's standing and decisions, one ticket with its body, attempts and lanes, and under the control scope a decision answered or a parked ticket resumed. The headset gets a Tickets tab on it.
- The headset reads what each stage produced: every attempt lists its notes and other artifacts, its checks log, its review rounds' findings and responses and its evidence, each opened with a tap as text or as a picture; a ticket's timeline is read from the runner's event log; and a closable ticket can be closed. The ticket list is ordered last moved first, with a menu for the order (waiting first, newest, by project), the hosts, projects and states (closed hidden unless asked) and a "waiting on me" switch.

### Changed

- The headset's conversation view follows the end as a mode: it is held at the end, nothing growing under it can leave it behind, and a button at the right edge releases it for reading; the ellipsis at the foot returns it to following. Before, a new turn that began with a tool call could push the end off screen and switch following off, and the view could jump up to the turn it last held at the top.

### Fixed

- The headset's filter menu no longer jumps back to its top every couple of seconds while open: it is rebuilt only when a host or a session state it lists changes, not on every refresh.

## [0.2.1] - 2026-10-15

### Fixed

- A first launch on a display macOS reports at an odd scale (a Sidecar
  screen) no longer aborts before the window shows: the GPU's own
  texture limit is asked for instead of egui's 8192 (#185).

## [0.2.0] - 2026-10-15

### Added

- The app's version in the Settings menu, with a check for a newer
  release on GitHub twenty seconds after launch and hourly after that.
  A newer one is offered for download, checked against its published
  checksum and the running app's signing team, and installed on
  "Restart to update", which quits, swaps the bundle in place and
  relaunches.
- The headset pairs with a discovered host by its typed code, with the
  host's key shown for a check by eye, since visionOS gives an app no
  camera.
- `scripts/bump.sh` and `scripts/release.sh`: the version, this
  changelog and a GitHub release with the signed bundle and its
  checksum.
- The host's `/info` reply names the app's version, and the headset
  shows it beside each known host.

## [0.1.0] - 2026-10-14

### Added

- The remote port and the visionOS client: pairing with a pinned key,
  sessions and working sets from several hosts, live screens,
  conversations, run output, the draft and dictation into the host's
  editor, commands under the control scope.
- The first GitHub release, built by hand.

input.old_string: So the pairing window shows a **QR code** carrying `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`, and under it the same in text: a short form of the key hash and the code. The client scans or types both; it connects, compares the hash of the key it is actually talking to with the one it was given, and only when they match sends `/pair {code, device_name, spki_sha256}`.
input.new_string: So the pairing window shows a **QR code** carrying the page's URL, `https://<address>:<port>/#code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>` (2026-10-23; before, the JSON `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`, which the Swift client's `PairingInvite.parse` still accepts), and under it the same in text: a short form of the key hash and the code. The three values travel in the URL's fragment, which a browser never sends in a request, so a server the owner has not verified never receives the code; the page compares `/info`'s key and id with the fragment's before it sends anything. The client scans or types both; it connects, compares the hash of the key it is actually talking to with the one it was given, and only when they match sends `/pair {code, device_name, spki_sha256}`. **A browser cannot pin**: it cannot see which certificate it is talking to, so the comparison catches a QR for another host or a stale one and is not a defence against a relay that terminates TLS; the trust step for a browser is proceeding past the certificate warning, and the dialog says to pair a browser only on a network you trust. The URL names the machine's local address only while the port listens on the network, and the loopback address otherwise, with the dialog saying the port is this Mac's alone.

input.old_string:
- **The token**: 32 bytes from the OS random source, base64url, 43 characters. It does not expire; the owner revokes. It is sent only as a bearer header over the pinned connection, never in a URL.
- `/pair` answers with the token and the granted scope. The host stores the device name, scope, created time, last-seen time and the token's SHA-256 in `<data dir>/devices.json` (atomic write, owner-readable); never the token. The client stores the token and the pinned key hash in its Keychain.
input.new_string:
- **The token**: 32 bytes from the OS random source, base64url, 43 characters. It does not expire; the owner revokes. It is sent only as a bearer header over the pinned connection, or as the cookie below, never in a URL.
- `/pair` answers with the token and the granted scope. The host stores the device name, scope, created time, last-seen time and the token's SHA-256 in `<data dir>/devices.json` (atomic write, owner-readable); never the token. The client stores the token and the pinned key hash in its Keychain.
- **A browser's credential is a cookie** (2026-10-23). `/pair` with `"transport": "cookie"` in its body answers with `Set-Cookie: __Host-sb-<server_id>=<token>; Max-Age=34560000; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` and a body without `token`, so the page's script never holds it; a native client omits the field and is unchanged. The host accepts the cookie named `__Host-sb-<its own server_id>` as a credential beside the bearer header (the bearer wins when both are present; every other cookie is ignored). The name carries the id because cookies ignore ports: two instances on one Mac share a jar for the page's host, and a fixed name would have the second pairing overwrite the first; the id is stable across a key rotation, so a rotation does not orphan the cookie. A request authenticated by the cookie alone that is not a `GET`, or is an upgrade, must carry `Origin: https://<Host header>`, else 403 `origin`: `SameSite=Strict` withholds the cookie cross-site, and this closes the same-site, other-port case. A bearer request needs no `Origin`. The browser keeps only `{server_id, spki_sha256, server_name}` in its storage, all public, which is what lets it tell a revocation (`/me` 401 with `/info` unchanged) from a changed identity (`/info` with another key or id); the host cannot say "revoked", since a revoked token and an unknown one are the same 401.

# Implement notes: #230 web control surface (v5rev-fable-leanb)

Branch `stage/sb-230-implement-v5rev-fable-leanb`, one commit as the
plan says, on top of `7fe8949` (Release 0.4.1). Not pushed, no PR.

## What was built

**Host transport (`src/adapters/remote.rs`).**
- `RemoteRequest` gained `cookie`, `origin`, `host` (the headers whole).
- `RemoteReply` gained `headers: Vec<(&'static str, String)>` and
  `RemoteReply::new(status, body, authenticated)`; the ten struct
  literals in `src/app.rs` and the one in the adapter were converted.
- `respond` now takes the reply's headers and every JSON reply carries
  `Cache-Control: no-store` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.
- The page paths (`GET /`, `/app.js`, `/app.css`, exact match) are
  answered in `connection` from `src/adapters/web.rs` with the CSP,
  `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, the two headers above and
  `Connection: close`; the thread returns after the reply, which frees
  the unauthenticated slot. `Limits.page` is a 120/min window, 429 past
  it. A `POST /`, `/favicon.ico`, `/index.html` still reach the frame
  and get the JSON 404.
- Small helpers `respond_error` and `respond_page`; `write_response`
  underneath both.

**App (`src/app.rs`).**
- `authenticate`: bearer if present, else the cookie named
  `__Host-sb-<this server_id>` (exact name, other cookies ignored). A
  cookie-authenticated non-`GET` or upgrade without
  `Origin: https://<Host>` is 403 `origin`; bearer requests exempt.
- `/pair` with `"transport": "cookie"` sets the cookie
  (`Max-Age=34560000; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict`) and
  omits `token` from the body; without it the reply is unchanged.
- `GET /api/v1/me` → `{device_id, name, scope, server_id, server_name}`
  under read scope. Not in `capabilities`.

**Core.** `core::remote::invite_url(identity, window, address, port)`,
re-exported from `core`; `None` address → `127.0.0.1`. IPv6 is
bracketed via `SocketAddr`'s Display. Core test added.

**UI (`src/ui/remote.rs`).** QR and "Copy invite" carry the URL. The
address is `local_address()` only when `identity.listen.lan` is on;
otherwise the Address line is replaced by a "This Mac only" notice.
The browser-trust sentence sits beside the redaction sentence. UI test
rewritten to assert the URL and the notice.

**Page (`web/`).** `index.html`, `app.js`, `app.css`, `app.test.js`.
Plain DOM, `textContent` only; API paths in one `API` table; the pure
parts (`parseFragment`, `deviceName`, `inferUnauthorized`, `accepts`,
`orderList`, `sinceText`, `newOp`) behind a guarded `module.exports`.
Boot → fragment → `replaceState` → `/info` compare → `/pair` cookie →
`/me` → list; no fragment → `/me`, 401 → the `/info` inference.
Polling `/waiting` every 3 s (20 s while the socket is up), socket
retry 5 s doubling to 60 s. Session view: `last-response` for `claude`,
`screen` otherwise; reply box under `control` with a null
`prompt_refusal`; op kept across a retry; 403 `scope` re-reads `/me`.

**Swift.** `PairingInvite.parse` takes the URL (host:port → address,
fragment → code/key/id, each required) and still the JSON; new
`InviteError`. Test added; `swift test --filter SwitchboardProtocolTests`
passes (5 tests). CLI usage line updated.

**Spike `spikes/23-web-page/`.** Standalone crate: a SAN-less rcgen
certificate, the CSP, `/pair` setting `__Host-sb-<id>`, `/me` echoing
it, a hand-rolled WebSocket 101 + one frame + close. Clippy-clean under
the pedantic set. README lists the five browser steps for the owner and
records **browser steps not run** (nothing here can drive a browser
past a certificate warning), plus the pool/window results from the
harness tests.

**Tests (`tests/remote.rs`).** New helpers `http_with`/`call_with`
(headers in and out), `pair_by_cookie`, `cookie_pair`, `header`;
`subscribe_at` now delegates to `subscribe_with(headers, path)`. Six
new tests: page headers and the 404s; page references only served
paths (href/src, every `/api/v1/` string in `app.js` answers for a
paired device, no inline script/handler/style, no innerHTML/eval/
document.write); cookie pairing incl. two hosts and the fixed-name
cookie; the Origin rule on send and upgrade; `/me` scope and revoke vs
`/info`; the page window (120 then 429, `/info` and `/pair`
unaffected); `node --test web/app.test.js` run from Rust, skipped if
node is absent. `stalled_strangers…` extended with a page request
failing at accept; the rotated-identity test now also reads `/info`.
Adapter unit test extended for the three new request fields;
`web.rs` has a table test.

**Docs.** `docs/remote-client.md` §0 dated line, §4.1 bullet, §4.3 two
rows, line 207 corrected (excerpt not on the port), §5 (pre-pairing
surface, URL invite with the fragment rationale and the browser's
weaker trust, the cookie bullet with the Origin rule). `docs/design.md`
dated paragraph with known gaps before "Versioning and updates".
README: dev-aid sentence, rows for `src/adapters/web.rs`, `web/`, the
spike, and updates to the `remote.rs` (adapter and UI) and
`tests/remote.rs` rows. CHANGELOG Unreleased line as the plan words it.

## Commits

One: "Serve a web control surface from the remote port, paired from a
URL whose fragment carries the code" with the plan's contract list in
the body.

## Checks

`cargo fmt --all`, `cargo clippy --locked --workspace --all-targets --
-D warnings`, `cargo test --locked --workspace` all clean before the
commit (the pre-commit hook runs them again). `swift test --filter
SwitchboardProtocolTests` passes. No `cfg(target_os)` arm was touched
and the dispatch crate is unchanged, so the Linux cross-check was not
needed. Node 24 is installed here, so the page test ran for real.

## Where the plan was wrong or needed a call

- **`serve_remote` and `connection` hit clippy's 100-line limit** with
  the additions. `/me` is one arm inside the existing body match;
  `connection`'s three error responses became a `respond_error`
  helper. No behaviour change.
- **"The implementer measures five parallel connections against the
  harness."** Done as deterministic assertions rather than a timing:
  120 sequential loads over the pool of four plus a `/info` after them
  (the slot was freed), and the stalled-strangers test extended with a
  page request failing at accept. A browser's own per-load connection
  count stays unmeasured (facts Unresolved 6); the spike README says so.
- **Spike browser steps could not be run** (no way to click through a
  certificate warning unattended); the README says "not run" as the
  plan allows, with the five steps spelled out for the owner.
- **The `Mac-only` test condition.** The plan says the notice shows
  "when `listen.lan` is off"; `Listen::default()` has `lan: false`, so
  the existing dialog test asserts it directly rather than a second
  test toggling the setting. The UI reads `identity.listen.lan` (the
  preference), not the bound listener, because `DrawCtx` carries only
  the port; the app rebinds on a change of listen, so they agree.
- **`Origin` comparison** is exact string `https://<Host>`; the test
  harness sends `Host: localhost`, so `Origin: https://localhost` is
  the own origin there. A browser sends the port in both.
- **`node` invocation from the agent shell was blocked by the sandbox's
  approval prompt**; the Rust test ran it under cargo instead, which is
  the path the plan names anyway.
- Line numbers in the plan were from `7fe8949`; the worktree was at
  the same commit, so nothing had moved.

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: Monitor
tools.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 10 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.
